You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

#!/usr/bin/env node
const { runExtract } = require("./index");

function parseArgs(argv) {
  const args = { input: null, outdir: null };
  for (let i = 0; i < argv.length; i += 1) {
    if (argv[i] === "--input" && argv[i + 1]) {
      args.input = argv[++i];
    } else if (argv[i] === "--outdir" && argv[i + 1]) {
      args.outdir = argv[++i];
    }
  }
  return args;
}

async function main() {
  const [command, ...rest] = process.argv.slice(2);
  if (command !== "extract") {
    process.stderr.write("usage: node src/cli.js extract --input <path> --outdir <dir>\n");
    process.exit(1);
  }
  const opts = parseArgs(rest);
  if (!opts.input || !opts.outdir) {
    process.stderr.write("missing --input or --outdir\n");
    process.exit(1);
  }
  try {
    await runExtract(opts.input, opts.outdir);
  } catch (err) {
    process.stderr.write(`${err.message}\n`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

Analysis: Repo and CLI were inspected. cli.js already validates command and missing args by writing to stderr and exiting 1. Running extract twice produced identical outputs (diff empty), so the reported “status drift between reruns” likely comes from unstable ordering/matching that only triggers when inputs have ties or when graders compare specific rows; we need to inspect reconciliation logic and the handbook in the archive to implement the correct matching rules (compliance holds incorporating later mail; correction notices applied to the correct ledger rows). We have not yet read the full handbook section nor reviewed reconcile/corrections/email parsers.
Plan: 1) Read the full handbook section from the archive to extract the precise reconciliation policy and exception rules. 2) Inspect parser modules (emails, corrections, ledger) and normalize/reconcile.js + normalize/exceptions.js to see current matching logic and where it can mis-attach corrections/holds. 3) Search the archive for keywords (HOLD, compliance, correction notice, ledger) to understand structures and required identifiers. 4) After identifying discrepancies vs handbook, patch the relevant modules (likely reconcile.js and corrections parser) to (a) build deterministic transaction keys, (b) model compliance holds as state that can be updated/cleared by later emails, and (c) apply corrections to specific ledger rows using the handbook’s linkage rule. 5) Re-run extractor into /app/output and validate outputs are stable and correct.

Analysis: The handbook in audit_archive.md defines strict reconciliation rules, but current code violates many: it locates sections via indexOf (explicitly forbidden), ledger parser keeps the first occurrence of a transaction_id (should take last non-provisional), ignores provisional flag, emails parser ignores sent: and compliance@ qualification/precedence rules, corrections parser uses indexOf section slicing and doesn’t resolve multiple notices by field with lexicographically greatest effective date, reconcile.js sets report.previous_value to empty and applies notices in input order, doesn’t implement owner amendments, status precedence rules, effective_date logic, exception_reason rules, or output formatting constraints (amount precision, exception join order, report sorting). Need to rewrite section parsing anchored to heading lines, implement proper reconciliation pipeline per handbook, and ensure writers match required JSON shapes and ordering.
Plan: 1) Inspect remaining parsers (policy exceptions, meetings amendments, sections) and writers to see current expectations and what needs changing. 2) Implement robust section extraction in parser/sections.js using regex anchored to whole heading lines (## / ####) to get exactly the intended sections; ensure only exact '## Transaction Ledger' is used and ledger-like decoys ignored. 3) Fix ledger parsing: parse multiple ledger blocks, skip provisional:true blocks, and for duplicate transaction_id keep the last non-provisional in file order. 4) Fix emails parsing: only apply status changes from From containing compliance@; parse optional sent: date; record it for later rule evaluation. 5) Parse meeting amendments: find '#### Amendment for TXN-<uuid>' blocks, only signed:true (case-insensitive); optional effective date must be >= ledger date to apply; these replace owner before corrections. 6) Parse policy exceptions: detect blocks for txn with approved_by: compliance. 7) Implement reconcileTransactions: start from base ledger rows; apply meeting amendments; apply qualifying email status changes with precedence and sent/ledger-date rule; then apply winning correction notices per (txn, field) by max lexicographic effective; compute reconciliation_report.jsonl entries with previous_value at time of application; update effective_date only when winning correction changes status or date (set to notice effective), otherwise keep ledger date. 8) Compute exception_reason per rules with semicolon-joined codes sorted lexically. 9) Ensure outputs: transactions.json/exceptions.json are {"items":[...]}; transactions sorted by transaction_id ascending; reconciliation_report.jsonl sorted by notice_id ascending; CSV formatting (2 decimals, blank exception when null). 10) Run extractor to /app/output with grader args.

Analysis: We inspected parsers and writers. They currently violate handbook requirements: sections located via indexOf; meetings amendments ignore signed/effective date rules and block boundaries; policy exceptions parser doesn’t check approved_by: compliance; jsonWriter uses keys transactions/exceptions instead of items; csvWriter missing exception_reason column and amount formatting; ledger/emails/corrections parsing incomplete. Also, apply_patch is not available in this environment, so edits must be done with heredocs (cat > file) or sed/perl. Next: rewrite several JS files accordingly and then run extractor to /app/output.
Plan: 1) Use cat heredocs to fully rewrite the small modules to match handbook: utils/sort.js, output/jsonWriter.js, output/csvWriter.js, parser helpers for section extraction, ledger/emails/corrections/meetings/policy, and normalize/reconcile.js + normalize/exceptions.js. 2) Implement a shared section extractor that uses regex anchored at line start for exact headings. 3) Update index.js remains mostly OK but will pick up corrected writers and reconcile logic. 4) Run node cli extract with grader args into /app/output and quickly inspect outputs (head) and run schema validation via existing validateOutputs (may need strengthening but not required).

Analysis: Core parsers and writers were rewritten to align with handbook structure requirements (anchored headings via extractSection, ledger last non-provisional, emails include sent, meetings include effective, policy requires approved_by compliance, corrections section parsing). Remaining major work: implement the actual reconciliation pipeline and exception logic in normalize/reconcile.js and normalize/exceptions.js, ensure reconciliation_report.jsonl sorting and previous_value tracking, implement effective_date rules, status precedence with compliance-only email qualification and sent>=ledger-date constraint, correction winning by lexicographically greatest effective per (txn,field), and exception_reason computations + joining. Also fix a small bug risk in sections.js: the regex literal contains \s that got interpreted as \s? It currently shows /^##\s+.../ correctly, but nextRe line has `^##\s+...` in file? Need to confirm. After reconciliation is fixed, run extractor into /app/output and spot-check outputs.
Plan: 1) Inspect current normalize/reconcile.js and normalize/exceptions.js to fully replace with handbook-compliant implementation. 2) Implement STATUS_ORDER and precedence compare; apply meeting amendments (signed true, effective null or >= ledger date). 3) Apply emails: only if from contains compliance@; if sent present require sent >= ledger date, and mark that txn had qualifying compliance email with sent for compliance_hold exception. If no sent, allow status update only if precedence allows (i.e., new status has >= precedence than current). 4) Determine winning correction notices: group by (transaction_id, field) and pick notice with max effective (lexicographic). Apply corrections after emails/amendments; for report, record previous_value at time of application; output report entries sorted by notice_id ascending. Track if winning correction changed status for retroactive_review exception. Also compute final effective_date per rule: start ledger date; if a winning correction changes status or date, set effective_date to that notice effective; else keep ledger date. 5) Implement buildExceptions to compute exception_reason codes and exceptions list. 6) Fix any remaining writer/schema issues. 7) Run extractor to /app/output and verify shapes/headers/order.
